sumatriptan.name: Sumatriptan
sumatriptan.summary: Sumatriptan is a medicine used to treat migraines and cluster headaches. It relieves the headache, feeling or being sick, and sensitivity to light and sound, but it does not stop migraines from starting. The NHS lists heart problems among the reasons it may not suit someone, and says a heart attack is a rare serious side effect that needs a 999 call.
usedFor: Treating migraine attacks, including the headache, feeling or being sick, and sensitivity to light and sound.
sumatriptan.howItWorks: Migraine symptoms may be caused by a temporary widening of blood vessels in the head. The NHS says sumatriptan is believed to reduce the widening of these blood vessels. It treats an attack that has begun and does not prevent migraines from starting. Sumatriptan belongs to the triptan group of migraine medicines.

common: The NHS lists feeling or being sick, dizziness, unsteadiness or tiredness, and flushing or feeling hot or cold as common side effects.
The NHS says common side effects are usually mild and do not last long.
The nasal spray can cause nosebleeds, irritation of the nose or throat and a bad taste, and the injection can cause bruising or swelling where it goes in.
The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using machinery while dizzy or tired after taking it.
serious: Anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) and a heart attack are listed by the NHS among serious side effects, and the NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance in these emergencies.
A heart attack can cause severe pain or tightness in the chest, and this needs a 999 call.
The NHS says confusion, muscle twitching, a high temperature or a fast heartbeat can be signs of serotonin syndrome, which needs a doctor to review it straight away.
For other serious side effects the NHS advises calling NHS 111.

cautions: The NHS lists coronary heart disease, angina, heart rhythm problems or a previous heart attack among the reasons sumatriptan may not be suitable.
Circulation problems in the legs, a past stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA), liver disease and seizures are also listed by the NHS as reasons for caution.
Most adults up to the age of 65 can take sumatriptan, and older adults sometimes can if a doctor prescribes it.
Sumatriptan is not officially approved for children, although a specialist doctor may sometimes prescribe it.
The NHS says taking too much can narrow blood vessels and lead to heart problems such as chest pain, an abnormal heart rhythm or a heart attack.
The NHS asks people to tell the prescriber about other migraine or headache medicines such as ergotamine or other triptans, and about antidepressants.
Using it with some antidepressants can cause serotonin syndrome, and a UK leaflet states that taking it with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant is not allowed.
St John's wort can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome, and the NHS advises against taking it with sumatriptan.
The NHS says there is not enough information to know how other herbal remedies, vitamins and supplements affect sumatriptan.
A UK leaflet says using sumatriptan too often may cause or worsen headaches, including when other painkillers are also needed regularly for migraine.
The NHS says sumatriptan is not thought to be harmful in pregnancy, but there is not enough research to say for certain.
The NHS says only very small amounts pass into breast milk and it is very unlikely to cause problems for a baby.
sumatriptan.monitoring: The sources used for this page do not describe routine blood tests for sumatriptan. A prescriber reviews whether it is controlling attacks and whether headaches have become frequent, because using it too often can cause or worsen headaches.

sections.heading: What is sumatriptan used for?
sections.body: Sumatriptan is used to treat migraines and cluster headaches. In a migraine attack it relieves the headache, feeling or being sick, and sensitivity to light and sound. It does not prevent migraines from starting, so it is a treatment for an attack that has begun. Triptans are generally taken once the headache has begun rather than during an aura, a trust leaflet says, because studies show they do not work as well if taken too early.

sections.heading: How does sumatriptan work?
sections.body: Migraine symptoms may be caused by a temporary widening of blood vessels in the head. The NHS says sumatriptan is believed to reduce this widening. It is available in different forms: the NHS describes tablets, a nasal spray and an injection.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: The common side effects the NHS lists are feeling or being sick, dizziness, unsteadiness, tiredness, and flushing or feeling hot or cold. The NHS says they are usually mild and do not last long. A heart attack and anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, are rare serious side effects, and the NHS says to call 999 and ask for an ambulance if either is suspected. The NHS says severe pain or tightness in the chest can be a sign of a heart attack. Other serious side effects are a reason to call NHS 111, according to the NHS.

sections.heading: Sumatriptan with other medicines and who needs extra care
sections.body: The NHS asks people to tell their prescriber about ergotamine, other triptans and antidepressants. Some antidepressants can cause serotonin syndrome when used with sumatriptan, and the NHS advises against St John's wort. Heart problems, a past stroke or TIA, circulation problems in the legs, liver disease and seizures are among the conditions the NHS lists as reasons it may not be suitable. The NHS says it is not thought to be harmful in pregnancy, but there is not enough research to say for certain.

faqs.q: Does sumatriptan stop migraines from happening?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says sumatriptan does not prevent migraines from starting. It relieves symptoms during an attack.

faqs.q: Can sumatriptan be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: Most sumatriptan is prescription only, but packs of 50 mg tablets can be bought from a pharmacy by adults who have previously been diagnosed with migraine. The injection and nasal spray are not sold over the counter, according to a local NHS formulary.

faqs.q: Can children or older people use sumatriptan?
faqs.a: Most adults up to the age of 65 can take it, and older adults sometimes can if a doctor prescribes it. It is not officially approved for children, although a specialist doctor may sometimes prescribe it.

faqs.q: What can happen if sumatriptan is used too often?
faqs.a: A UK leaflet says using it too often may cause or worsen headaches. The NHS says taking too much can narrow blood vessels and cause heart problems.

ondansetron.name: Ondansetron
ondansetron.summary: Ondansetron is an anti-sickness medicine used to prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery. It belongs to the 5-HT3 receptor antagonist group, and the main cautions are an effect on the heart rhythm (QT prolongation) and use in early pregnancy.
usedFor: Preventing nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy or radiotherapy, with age limits that differ between the two uses.
Preventing nausea and vomiting after surgery.
ondansetron.howItWorks: Ondansetron is a specific 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, which blocks 5-HT3 receptors in the gut and in the central nervous system. MedlinePlus says medicines in this group work by blocking serotonin, a natural substance that may cause nausea and vomiting.

common: Headache is very common with ondansetron, according to a UK leaflet.
Constipation and flushing or a feeling of warmth are also listed as common.
Hiccups, low blood pressure and an irregular heartbeat are listed as uncommon effects.
serious: A UK leaflet lists allergic reactions, chest pain and heart rhythm disturbances among the serious effects that call for medical help.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: A UK leaflet says ondansetron must not be used with apomorphine (a Parkinson's disease medicine) or by anyone allergic to it.
The solution leaflet rules out use in the first three months of pregnancy.
The MHRA has warned of a small increased risk of cleft lip or palate after first-trimester use, and says women should be counselled on benefits and risks before it is offered.
An NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service page says ondansetron can be used with caution during breastfeeding, with monitoring of the baby.
Leaflets advise caution in people with a bowel blockage or severe constipation, heart failure, heart rhythm problems, liver problems or abnormal blood levels of potassium, sodium or magnesium.

An NHS prescribing sheet says ondansetron lengthens the QT interval (a measure of the heart's electrical cycle) in a dose-related way, and that torsade de pointes, a dangerous heart rhythm, has been reported, mainly with high intravenous doses.

The same sheet advises avoiding it in congenital long QT syndrome, and caution with heart failure, slow heart rates, other QT-prolonging medicines, and low potassium or magnesium, which are corrected before use.
The sheet also warns of serotonin syndrome when ondansetron is combined with medicines such as SSRIs, SNRIs and opioids.
ondansetron.monitoring: An NHS prescribing sheet says low potassium and magnesium are corrected before use. A prescriber considers heart rhythm risk when other QT-prolonging medicines are used.

sections.heading: What is ondansetron used for?
sections.body: A UK tablet leaflet lists two licensed uses for ondansetron: preventing nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and preventing it after surgery. MedlinePlus gives the same two groups of uses for adults taking the tablets. Great Ormond Street Hospital describes it as a medicine that stops a child feeling sick and being sick. It may be given by mouth as a tablet, melt or syrup, or as an injection into a vein.

sections.heading: How does ondansetron work?
sections.body: Serotonin is a natural substance that can trigger nausea and vomiting. Ondansetron blocks 5-HT3 receptors for serotonin in the gut and in the central nervous system. Medicines in this group are called 5-HT3 receptor antagonists. Great Ormond Street Hospital notes that some medicines can react with ondansetron and change how well it works, so a doctor or pharmacist is asked about other medicines first.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: Headache is listed as very common, and constipation and flushing as common. Allergic reactions, chest pain and heart rhythm disturbances are among the serious effects listed in a UK leaflet. These need urgent medical help: call 999 for an emergency, or NHS 111 for urgent advice.

sections.heading: Heart rhythm, pregnancy and other cautions
sections.body: Ondansetron lengthens the QT interval in a dose-related way, according to an NHS prescribing sheet. The sheet advises avoiding it in congenital long QT syndrome and taking care with low potassium or magnesium, heart failure, slow heart rates and other QT-prolonging medicines. The MHRA has reported a small increased risk of cleft lip or palate with first-trimester use. Apomorphine must not be used with ondansetron, according to a UK leaflet.

faqs.q: Is ondansetron available without a prescription?
faqs.a: No. Ondansetron is a prescription-only medicine in the UK, according to the emc legal category.

faqs.q: Can ondansetron affect the heart?
faqs.a: Yes. An NHS prescribing sheet says it lengthens the QT interval in a dose-related way. Torsade de pointes has been reported, mainly with high intravenous doses.

faqs.q: Can ondansetron be used while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: An NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service page says it can be used with caution, with monitoring of the baby.

metoclopramide.name: Metoclopramide
metoclopramide.summary: Metoclopramide is an anti-sickness medicine used to stop nausea (feeling sick) and vomiting (being sick), including the sickness that can come with a migraine. The MHRA has restricted its dose and duration to reduce the risk of serious neurological side effects, so it is prescribed for short-term use only.
usedFor: Treating the sickness that can happen during a migraine.

In children aged 1 to 18 the MHRA says it is used only as a second-line option, for preventing delayed nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy and for treating established nausea and vomiting after surgery.
metoclopramide.howItWorks: Metoclopramide belongs to a group of anti-sickness medicines that block dopamine. The retrieved NHS and regulator pages do not describe its mechanism in more detail.

common: The NHS says the most common side effects are feeling sleepy (drowsy) and diarrhoea.
Low mood, tremors and tics are also reported.
Leaflets say it may affect vision and the ability to drive or use machines.
serious: The NHS says the most common serious side effect is uncontrollable movements, such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms.
The MHRA says the risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: The NHS says metoclopramide suits most adults and children aged 1 year or over.
Epilepsy, Parkinson's disease and a past allergic reaction to it are listed by the NHS as reasons it may not suit someone.
Formularies list gastrointestinal obstruction, perforation or bleeding as reasons not to use it, and say it is not used in children under 1 year.

The NHS asks people taking medicines for Parkinson's disease such as levodopa, medicines that cause drowsiness such as diazepam or amitriptyline, or other anti-sickness medicines to speak to a doctor or pharmacist first.
The NHS says herbal remedies and supplements have not been shown to be safe to take with it, and some can make side effects worse.
The NHS does not recommend drinking alcohol with it because this increases the risk of side effects.
metoclopramide.monitoring: The NHS says treatment is usually for a short time because longer use can cause side effects. A prescriber reviews the need for it, because the MHRA limits its use to short-term treatment.

sections.heading: What is metoclopramide used for?
sections.body: The NHS describes metoclopramide as a prescription-only medicine that stops nausea and vomiting. It is also prescribed for the sickness that can happen during a migraine. The NHS says it suits most adults and children aged 1 year or over. NHS formularies list gastrointestinal obstruction, perforation or bleeding as reasons not to use it.

sections.heading: The MHRA restriction on short-term use
sections.body: The MHRA reviewed the neurological risks of metoclopramide and restricted its dose and duration of use, to reduce the risk of serious neurological side effects. The review confirmed known risks such as short-term movement disorders (extrapyramidal disorders) and tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder that can persist. As a result it is prescribed only for short-term use, and the NHS says it is usually prescribed for a short time because side effects can occur with longer use. The risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults, and the MHRA says it is not used in children under 1 year.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: The NHS lists drowsiness and diarrhoea as the most common side effects. The most common serious effect is uncontrollable movement such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms. Such movements need prompt medical advice: NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and 999 if breathing or swallowing is affected.

sections.heading: Other medicines and who needs extra care
sections.body: The NHS asks people to check with a doctor or pharmacist before combining metoclopramide with Parkinson's disease medicines, medicines that cause drowsiness or other anti-sickness medicines. Alcohol is not recommended with it because it increases the risk of side effects. Epilepsy and Parkinson's disease are listed by the NHS as conditions where it may not be suitable.

faqs.q: How long can metoclopramide be taken?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is usually prescribed for a short time because it can cause side effects with longer use, and the MHRA restricts it to short-term use.

faqs.q: Is metoclopramide used in children?
faqs.a: The MHRA says that in children aged 1 to 18 it is only a second-line option for two uses, and it is not used under 1 year.

faqs.q: Can metoclopramide be used for migraine?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is also prescribed for the sickness that can happen during a migraine.

loperamide.name: Loperamide
loperamide.summary: Loperamide is a medicine for diarrhoea that slows the activity of the bowel so that stools firm up. It can help with short-term diarrhoea and, in adults with a doctor's diagnosis, irritable bowel syndrome, and it is not suitable for everyone. Taking more than recommended can cause serious heart problems, and the NHS says a fast, irregular or pounding heartbeat needs urgent help.
usedFor: Helping with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in adults whose doctor has diagnosed it.
Treating longer-lasting diarrhoea from conditions such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, on prescription.
loperamide.howItWorks: The NHS says loperamide works by slowing the activity of the bowel. Bowel contents then move more slowly and stay in the intestine for longer, which lets more water be absorbed back into the body and firms up stools. The US FDA describes loperamide as acting on opioid receptors in the gut to slow movement through the intestine.

common: The NHS lists headache, dizziness, constipation, feeling sick and wind as common side effects.
The NHS says loperamide can cause dizziness, tiredness and drowsiness, and that drinking alcohol makes these more likely.
The NHS advises against driving or using machinery if affected.
serious: The NHS says signs of a serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face, lips or throat or difficulty breathing, need urgent help, and that a 999 call is the route for an emergency.
MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount of loperamide can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal.
The NHS lists a fast, irregular or pounding heartbeat, bloody stools, severe stomach pain or swelling, and fever as signs to get medical help.
The US FDA says that at much higher than recommended amounts loperamide can cause severe heart rhythm problems and death.

cautions: Over the counter, the NHS says loperamide is for anyone aged 12 or over with short-term diarrhoea, and for adults with IBS only if a doctor has diagnosed it.
Children aged 11 or under and adults with long-lasting diarrhoea need a prescription, according to the NHS.

The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis or another inflammatory bowel condition, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature among the situations where it is not suitable.
The NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough evidence about it, and that anyone pregnant should speak to a doctor first.
The NHS says breastfeeding is considered acceptable because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk and no side effects are expected in the baby.
The NHS says some medicines can affect how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil, desmopressin and other anti-diarrhoea or bowel medicines.
The NHS says loperamide can be taken alongside paracetamol or ibuprofen and does not stop contraceptive pills working, although severe diarrhoea can make the pill less reliable.
loperamide.monitoring: Loperamide for long-lasting diarrhoea or bowel conditions is supervised by a doctor.

sections.heading: What is loperamide used for?
sections.body: The NHS describes loperamide as a medicine to treat diarrhoea. It can help with short-term diarrhoea and with irritable bowel syndrome that a doctor has diagnosed in an adult. For longer-lasting diarrhoea, such as that from Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, it is available on prescription.

sections.heading: How does loperamide work?
sections.body: Loperamide slows the activity of the bowel, so the contents move more slowly and stay in the intestine for longer. More water is then absorbed back into the body and stools become firmer. The NHS says it usually starts to improve diarrhoea within 1 hour.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: Common side effects listed by the NHS are headache, dizziness, constipation, feeling sick and wind. Dizziness, tiredness and drowsiness are more likely with alcohol. A fast, irregular or pounding heartbeat can be a sign of heart problems from taking too much. Swelling of the face, lips or throat, or difficulty breathing, is an emergency: call 999. Bloody stools, severe stomach pain or swelling, or fever need medical advice: NHS 111 or a GP the same day.

sections.heading: Who should not use loperamide, and other medicines
sections.body: The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis or similar conditions, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature as situations where it is not suitable. Pregnancy is a situation where the NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended and a doctor should be consulted first. Several medicines can change how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil and desmopressin.

faqs.q: Can loperamide be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: Yes, for people aged 12 or over with short-term diarrhoea, according to the NHS.

faqs.q: Can too much loperamide be harmful?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal. A fast, irregular or pounding heartbeat needs urgent medical help.

faqs.q: Is loperamide suitable in pregnancy and breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is not usually recommended in pregnancy, and that breastfeeding is considered acceptable.

loperamide.onset: The NHS says loperamide usually starts to make diarrhoea better within 1 hour.

lactulose.name: Lactulose
lactulose.summary: Lactulose is a laxative used to treat constipation, and it is also used in hepatic encephalopathy, a liver condition that causes confusion. The NHS says it draws water into the bowel to make poo softer, and that it takes at least 2 days to work.
usedFor: Treating hepatic encephalopathy, a liver disease that causes confusion, tremor and a decreased level of consciousness.
lactulose.howItWorks: The NHS says lactulose relieves constipation by drawing water into the bowel, which makes poo softer. Osmotic laxatives such as lactulose retain water in the bowel, which increases the volume of the stools and makes them softer and easier to pass, according to local NHS laxative guidance.

common: The NHS says diarrhoea, particularly with high amounts, is a very common side effect.
Bloating and wind are also common, and these effects are usually mild and do not last long.
serious: The NHS says serious side effects are rare, and that anaphylaxis, a serious allergic reaction, is possible in rare cases.
Long-term use can lead to prolonged diarrhoea and an imbalance of body salts (electrolytes).
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: The NHS says most people aged 14 and over can use lactulose, and that children under 14 need a doctor to prescribe it.
The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to lactulose or a similar medicine, galactosaemia, lactose intolerance and galactose or fructose allergies as reasons to avoid it.
Irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease, Crohn's disease and a bowel blockage that is not caused by constipation are conditions where the NHS advises checking first.
The NHS says lactulose increases gas and bloating, which can make IBS worse.
For people with diabetes, the NHS says usual constipation amounts should have little or no effect on blood sugar, but high amounts taken for many months might.
The NHS says lactulose can be taken during pregnancy and is not harmful to the baby, and that breastfeeding is fine if a doctor or midwife says the baby is healthy.
The NHS says contraceptive pills may not protect against pregnancy if lactulose makes someone vomit or causes severe diarrhoea.
lactulose.monitoring: A doctor reviews constipation that has not improved after 4 or 5 days of lactulose, according to the NHS. For hepatic encephalopathy, treatment is directed by a clinician and diarrhoea-related dehydration is a concern.

sections.heading: What is lactulose used for?
sections.body: The NHS lists two uses for lactulose: constipation and hepatic encephalopathy. Hepatic encephalopathy is a liver disease that causes confusion, tremor and a decreased level of consciousness. The NHS says lactulose is available on prescription and can also be bought from pharmacies. Babies and children under 14 need a doctor to prescribe it, according to the NHS.

sections.heading: How does lactulose work, and how long does it take?
sections.body: Lactulose draws water into the bowel, which makes poo softer. It is slow-acting and takes at least 2 days to work. The NHS says to talk to a doctor if constipation has not improved after 4 or 5 days. Local NHS guidance describes osmotic laxatives as retaining water in the bowel, which increases the volume of the stools and makes them softer and easier to pass.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: Diarrhoea, bloating and wind are the common side effects. They are usually mild and do not last long. Serious side effects are rare, but long-term use can cause prolonged diarrhoea and an imbalance of electrolytes. A serious allergic reaction is an emergency: call 999. For other worries, NHS 111 or a GP can advise.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with lactulose?
sections.body: Children under 14 need a doctor to prescribe it, according to the NHS. Lactose intolerance, galactosaemia and galactose or fructose allergies are listed as reasons to avoid it. People with irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease or Crohn's disease are advised to check first, because lactulose increases gas and bloating. The NHS says it can be taken during pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can lactulose be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says it is available on prescription and can be bought from pharmacies.

faqs.q: Does lactulose affect blood sugar?
faqs.a: The NHS says usual constipation amounts should have little or no effect, but high amounts taken for many months might.

faqs.q: Can lactulose be used for liver problems?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS lists hepatic encephalopathy, a liver disease that causes confusion, as one of its uses.

lactulose.onset: The NHS says lactulose takes at least 2 days to work, and that anyone whose constipation has not improved after 4 or 5 days should talk to a doctor.

diazepam.name: Diazepam
diazepam.summary: Diazepam is a benzodiazepine, a type of medicine used to treat anxiety, muscle spasms and seizures. The NHS says it should only be used for the short term, and that longer use can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms. It is a controlled drug in the UK, and the NHS advises against driving, cycling or using machinery while it affects alertness.
diazepam.howItWorks: NHS Inform describes benzodiazepines as depressant drugs that slow down the central nervous system. The sources used for this page do not describe the mechanism in more detail.

common: The NHS lists feeling less alert, increased anxiety and depression, drowsiness, tiredness and low blood pressure as common side effects.
The NHS advises against alcohol and grapefruit juice while taking diazepam because they can increase the risk of side effects.
The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while affected.
serious: Rare serious side effects listed by the NHS include a severe allergic reaction, slowed breathing and yellowing of the skin or eyes.
NHS Inform says stopping benzodiazepines suddenly can cause withdrawal effects that could be life-threatening.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: The NHS says taking diazepam for longer than the short term can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms.
NHS Inform says tolerance can develop quickly and there is a risk of psychological and physical dependence.
The MHRA says dependence can occur with therapeutic doses of benzodiazepines and can become established within weeks.
NHS Inform says benzodiazepines slow the central nervous system, which increases the risk of overdose, particularly when combined with alcohol, gabapentinoids or opioids.

The NHS lists long-term kidney, liver, heart or breathing problems, certain mental health conditions, a history of alcohol or drug misuse and a past allergic reaction to diazepam or similar medicines as reasons for care.
The NHS advises against diazepam in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it, and says regular use late in pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby after birth.
The NHS says diazepam passes into breast milk in small amounts, and advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor before use while breastfeeding.
diazepam.monitoring: A prescriber reviews the need for diazepam early, because the NHS says it should only be used for the short term. Reducing use gradually is the approach NHS Inform describes after longer use, rather than stopping suddenly.

sections.heading: What is diazepam used for?
sections.body: The NHS says diazepam is a benzodiazepine used to treat anxiety, muscle spasms and seizures. It is available only on prescription. NHS Inform describes benzodiazepines as depressant drugs that slow down the central nervous system.

sections.heading: Dependence, withdrawal and stopping
sections.body: The NHS says diazepam should only be used for the short term, and that taking it for longer can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms. NHS Inform says tolerance can develop quickly, with a risk of psychological and physical dependence. The MHRA says dependence can occur at therapeutic doses and can become established within weeks. If benzodiazepines are stopped suddenly, withdrawal effects can occur, and NHS Inform says these could be life-threatening. Because of this, reduction after longer use is gradual and planned with the prescriber; a GP appointment is the route, and NHS 111 or 999 if withdrawal symptoms are severe.

sections.heading: Driving, alcohol and side effects
sections.body: The NHS lists feeling less alert, drowsiness, tiredness and low blood pressure among common side effects. The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while affected. Alcohol and grapefruit juice can increase the risk of side effects, according to the NHS. Rare serious side effects include a severe allergic reaction, slowed breathing and yellowing of the skin or eyes.

sections.heading: Controlled drug status and who needs extra care
sections.body: Diazepam is a Class C drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and is in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. The NHS lists long-term kidney, liver, heart or breathing problems, certain mental health conditions and a history of alcohol or drug misuse among the reasons for care. It is not advised in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist recommends it, and the NHS says regular use late in pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby. NHS Inform warns that combining benzodiazepines with alcohol, gabapentinoids or opioids raises the risk of overdose.

faqs.q: How long can diazepam be taken?
faqs.a: The NHS says it should only be used for the short term, because longer use can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms.

faqs.q: Is diazepam a controlled drug?
faqs.a: Yes. It is Class C under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001.

faqs.q: Can diazepam be drunk with alcohol?
faqs.a: The NHS advises against alcohol with diazepam because it can increase the risk of side effects.

zopiclone.name: Zopiclone
zopiclone.summary: Zopiclone is a medicine used to treat insomnia, usually prescribed for just 2 to 4 weeks. The NHS says the body gets used to it quickly and that dependence is possible with longer use, and it advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking it. It is a controlled drug in the UK (Schedule 4 Part 1, Class C).
usedFor: Short-term treatment of insomnia in adults.
The NHS describes it as treatment for severe insomnia.
zopiclone.howItWorks: The sources used for this page do not describe how zopiclone works beyond calling it a sleeping medicine for insomnia. The NHS says caffeine has the opposite effect to zopiclone in the body and stops it working.

common: The NHS lists a metallic or bitter taste, a dry mouth and daytime sleepiness as common side effects.
Some people have been reported to sleepwalk, or to eat or make phone calls while asleep.
The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking zopiclone.
serious: The NHS lists difficulty breathing, allergic reactions, sleepwalking or other activity while not fully awake, hallucinations and low mood among serious side effects.
The summary of product characteristics says treatment should stop immediately if a complex sleep behaviour such as sleepwalking occurs.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: The NHS says alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep, so that breathing is not normal and waking is very difficult.
The NHS says combining it with opioid painkillers or other sedating medicines can cause problems, and that cannabis, heroin or methadone can intensify its sedative effects.

The NHS says most adults over 18 can take zopiclone, and lists a past allergic reaction, liver or kidney problems, myasthenia gravis, breathing problems or sleep apnoea, a history of mental health problems and past alcohol or drug misuse as reasons for care.
A UK leaflet and the summary of product characteristics say it should not be used by anyone who has previously had complex sleep behaviours with it.
The NHS says taking it in pregnancy may cause drowsiness or withdrawal symptoms such as agitation or shaking in the newborn.
The NHS says zopiclone has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies, though there is a very small risk of sleepiness.
The NHS says stopping suddenly can bring back insomnia, with anxiety and restlessness, although withdrawal symptoms are unlikely after less than a month of use.
zopiclone.monitoring: The NHS says zopiclone is usually prescribed for only 2 to 4 weeks, because the body gets used to it quickly. A prescriber reviews the need for it, because it is licensed for short-term use.

sections.heading: What is zopiclone used for?
sections.body: The NHS describes zopiclone as a medicine used to treat insomnia. The summary of product characteristics gives short-term treatment of insomnia in adults as its licensed use. The NHS says it is usually prescribed for only 2 to 4 weeks, because the body gets used to it quickly.

sections.heading: Dependence and stopping
sections.body: The NHS says someone taking zopiclone for up to 4 weeks is unlikely to become addicted, and may become dependent if it is taken for longer. The NHS says it should not be stopped suddenly without speaking to a doctor. Withdrawal can bring back insomnia, with anxiety and restlessness, but symptoms are unlikely in people who have taken it for less than a month. A GP appointment is the route for questions about stopping, and NHS 111 or 999 if symptoms are severe.

sections.heading: Driving, alcohol and sleep behaviours
sections.body: The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking zopiclone. Alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep, with breathing that is not normal and great difficulty waking. Some people have sleepwalked, or eaten or made phone calls while asleep, and the summary of product characteristics says treatment should stop immediately if this happens. Caffeine has the opposite effect to zopiclone and can stop it working, the NHS says.

sections.heading: Side effects and who needs extra care
sections.body: Common side effects listed by the NHS are a metallic taste, a dry mouth and daytime sleepiness. The NHS lists difficulty breathing, allergic reactions, hallucinations and low mood among serious side effects. Liver or kidney problems, myasthenia gravis, breathing problems or sleep apnoea, a history of mental health problems and past alcohol or drug misuse are listed by the NHS as reasons for care. Zopiclone is a Class C drug in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations.

faqs.q: Is zopiclone addictive?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to zopiclone, and that people taking it for up to 4 weeks are unlikely to become addicted.

faqs.q: Is zopiclone a controlled drug?
faqs.a: Yes. It is Class C and in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations, from June 2014.

faqs.q: Can zopiclone be taken with alcohol?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep with breathing problems and difficulty waking.

triptans.name: Triptans
triptans.summary: Triptans are medicines for treating migraine attacks, and sumatriptan is the triptan covered on this site. The NHS says sumatriptan relieves symptoms of migraine but does not prevent migraines from starting.
triptans.mechanism: The NHS says migraine symptoms may be caused by a temporary widening of blood vessels in the head, and sumatriptan is believed to reduce this widening.
cautions: Heart problems, a past stroke or transient ischaemic attack, circulation problems in the legs and liver disease are listed by the NHS as reasons sumatriptan may not be suitable.
Combining sumatriptan with some antidepressants or St John's wort can cause serotonin syndrome, according to the NHS and UK leaflets.

5-ht3-receptor-antagonists.name: 5-HT3 receptor antagonists
5-ht3-receptor-antagonists.summary: 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are anti-sickness medicines; ondansetron is the member covered on this site. Ondansetron is used to prevent nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery.
5-ht3-receptor-antagonists.mechanism: They block 5-HT3 receptors for serotonin in the gut and the central nervous system.
cautions: It may be given by mouth as a tablet, melt or syrup, or as an injection into a vein, according to Great Ormond Street Hospital.
The MHRA has warned of a small increased risk of cleft lip or palate after first-trimester use of ondansetron.
A UK leaflet says ondansetron must not be used with apomorphine.
An NHS prescribing sheet says ondansetron lengthens the QT interval in a dose-related way and is avoided in congenital long QT syndrome.

references.title: emc: Ondansetron 4 mg film-coated tablets package leaflet

dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics.name: Dopamine antagonist anti-sickness medicines
dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics.summary: Dopamine antagonist anti-sickness medicines are used to treat nausea and vomiting, and metoclopramide is the member covered on this site. The MHRA has restricted metoclopramide to short-term use because of the risk of serious neurological side effects.
dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics.mechanism: Metoclopramide is grouped with domperidone in NHS formularies, and the sources used here do not describe the group's mechanism in more detail.
cautions: The MHRA says the risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults, and that in children aged 1 to 18 it is only a second-line option.
Epilepsy and Parkinson's disease are listed by the NHS as conditions where metoclopramide may not suit someone.
The NHS asks people taking Parkinson's disease medicines, drowsiness-causing medicines or other anti-sickness medicines to speak to a doctor or pharmacist first.
The NHS says uncontrollable movements such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms are the most common serious side effect of metoclopramide.

references.title: MHRA: Metoclopramide: risk of neurological adverse effects

antimotility-agents.name: Antimotility agents
antimotility-agents.summary: Antimotility agents are medicines that slow the bowel to treat diarrhoea, and loperamide is the member covered on this site. The NHS says loperamide works by slowing the bowel so that more water is absorbed and stools firm up.
antimotility-agents.mechanism: The US FDA describes loperamide as acting on opioid receptors in the gut to slow movement through the intestine.
cautions: The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature as situations where loperamide is not suitable.
The NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough evidence about it.
The NHS says some medicines can affect how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil and desmopressin.
MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount of loperamide can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal.

osmotic-laxatives.name: Osmotic laxatives
osmotic-laxatives.summary: Osmotic laxatives hold water in the bowel to soften stools, and lactulose is the member covered on this site. Local NHS guidance describes osmotic laxatives as retaining water, which increases stool volume and makes stools softer and easier to pass.
osmotic-laxatives.mechanism: The NHS says lactulose draws water into the bowel, which makes poo softer.
cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to lactulose, galactosaemia, lactose intolerance and galactose or fructose allergies as reasons to avoid it.
Irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease, Crohn's disease and a bowel blockage not caused by constipation are conditions where the NHS advises checking first.
The NHS says high amounts taken for many months might affect blood sugar in people with diabetes.
Diarrhoea, bloating and wind are common with lactulose, according to the NHS.

benzodiazepines.name: Benzodiazepines
benzodiazepines.summary: Benzodiazepines are depressant medicines that slow the central nervous system, and diazepam is the member covered on this site. The MHRA says dependence can occur with therapeutic doses and can become established within weeks.
benzodiazepines.mechanism: NHS Inform describes benzodiazepines as drugs that slow down the central nervous system.
cautions: The NHS advises against alcohol and grapefruit juice while taking diazepam because they can increase the risk of side effects.
The NHS advises against diazepam in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it, and says regular use late in pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby.
NHS Inform says combining benzodiazepines with alcohol, gabapentinoids or opioids raises the risk of overdose.
NHS Inform says stopping benzodiazepines suddenly can cause withdrawal effects that could be life-threatening.
Licensed benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam and clonazepam are Class C drugs listed in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations.

z-drugs.name: Z-drugs
z-drugs.summary: Z-drugs are sleeping medicines used for insomnia, and zopiclone is the member covered on this site. NICE technology appraisal TA77 covers zaleplon, zolpidem and zopiclone for short-term insomnia.
z-drugs.mechanism: The sources used for this page do not describe the mechanism of Z-drugs.
cautions: The NHS says alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep, so that breathing is not normal and waking is very difficult.
The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking zopiclone.
The NHS says the body gets used to zopiclone quickly, which is why it is usually prescribed for only 2 to 4 weeks.
The summary of product characteristics for zopiclone says treatment should stop immediately if a complex sleep behaviour such as sleepwalking occurs.
Zopiclone is a Class C drug in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations.
